entry.title: Building an Agentic Kubernetes Platform That Runs Anywhere
entry.summary: A deep dive into an event-driven, portable agent platform that combines Kafka coordination, Cilium networking, GPU model serving, governed analytics, knowledge graphs, and reproducible AWS, Proxmox, and Kind deployment paths.
entry.content:
The Agentic Kubernetes Platform is an Apache-2.0 reference architecture for running specialist agents, model inference, and training without tying the application contract to one cloud. It uses the same agent protocol on AWS EKS and Proxmox-hosted Kubernetes; only the capacity, identity, load-balancing, and object-storage adapters change.

The core design decision: events between agents

Direct HTTP calls produce a deceptively simple demo but tightly couple agent availability, retry behavior, and scaling. Here, the supervisor discovers an exact skill from an Agent Card, publishes a JSON-RPC 2.0 request to the agent's Kafka topic, and correlates the response from results.* using the request ID.

client → Cilium Gateway → supervisor → tasks.weather
                                      → weather worker
client ← supervisor ← results.weather ←┘

Workers publish their result before committing the input offset. That gives the system an explicit at-least-once contract. It does not make an external weather API, Neo4j, and Kafka one transaction, so each handler must use the request or document ID as an idempotency key. This is a more useful production contract than pretending distributed side effects are exactly once.

Every specialist owns a directory, versioned Agent Card, task/result topics, domain implementation, container, and focused tests. The shared runtime owns JSON-RPC validation, manual Kafka commits, Redis caching, Prometheus metrics, and optional MLflow traces. Domain behavior remains outside the framework.

Three specialists demonstrate different workloads

The weather agent is intentionally lightweight. It resolves imperfect location phrasing through Open-Meteo, serves current conditions and forecasts, and caches repeated reads. It demonstrates the minimum useful agent contract without requiring an LLM.

The knowledge-graph agent demonstrates expensive asynchronous work. Its API stores an uploaded PDF, text, or JSON document in S3 or RustFS and sends only a durable URI and metadata through Kafka. A KEDA-scaled worker extracts bounded chunks through an OpenAI-compatible model, validates entities and relationships against a versioned ontology, writes graph truth to Neo4j, and indexes semantic candidates in Qdrant. The included explorer renders the result in 2D or 3D and traces shortest paths with evidence back to the source object.

The analytics agent delegates governed questions such as analytics.usage to Cube Core. It never accepts arbitrary SQL. Instead it constructs a bounded semantic query, adds the authenticated conversation owner as a tenant filter, signs a short-lived Cube JWT, and returns both rows and the exact query for reproduction. The sibling Cube operator owns Cube API, refresh worker, and Cube Store lifecycle.

Conversations, identity, and model routing

The minimal dashboard is deliberately not another runtime. It calls the same supervisor API, persists user and pending assistant messages in PostgreSQL, and polls until a correlated Kafka result completes the response. Read-only sharing uses a rotatable 256-bit token; PostgreSQL stores only its SHA-256 digest.

Cognito is the managed AWS identity provider, while the bare-metal profile uses the Keycloak Operator. APIs derive tenant identity from verified OIDC claims, not request parameters. Redis remains disposable cache, PostgreSQL owns relational workflow state, Neo4j owns explicit relationships, Qdrant owns rebuildable vectors, and S3/RustFS owns durable source artifacts.

The supervisor's LLM gateway is a visible, replaceable component. A local Apple Silicon environment can route prompts through an MLX-hosted Qwen 27B 4-bit model; GPU clusters use an OpenAI-compatible endpoint such as vLLM. Named skills still work when the router model is absent. Bring Your Own Agent requires only a valid Agent Card and Kafka contract; Bring Your Own Model requires an internal OpenAI-compatible endpoint and explicit registration.

Portable infrastructure without pretending it is identical

The two targets share Cilium CNI, NetworkPolicy, Envoy, Gateway API, Kafka, KEDA, Helm packaging, and agent contracts. Their infrastructure adapters differ:

Concern AWS Bare metal
Kubernetes EKS K3s on Proxmox VMs
Identity Cognito Keycloak Operator
Public address AWS load balancer MetalLB
Durable objects S3 RustFS S3-compatible API
GPU capacity Autoscaled NVIDIA nodes Passed-through local NVIDIA cards

Object storage is the durable source for models and datasets. An init container hydrates a PVC or local NVMe cache concurrently and atomically, so restarts can reuse warm files rather than repeatedly downloading from an external model registry. This improves startup only when the cache is retained and networking is appropriately provisioned; the project does not claim storage eliminates model-loading time.

Reproduce it locally

Docker Compose is the shortest application-level path:

git clone https://github.com/sqe/agentic-kubernetes-platform.git
cd agentic-kubernetes-platform
make install && make test
docker compose up --build
open http://localhost:8002/dashboard

Kind exercises the Kubernetes topology, including Cilium Gateway API, Redpanda's Kafka-compatible API, KEDA, RustFS, PostgreSQL, Qdrant, Neo4j, Redis, and operator-managed Keycloak:

make kind-up
make kind-status
curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8080/knowledge/health
open http://127.0.0.1:8080/dashboard
make kind-down

The repository separates source checks from deployment evidence. Unit tests, Helm rendering, Terraform validation, and Compose validation prove only their stated scope. Runtime evidence should include request IDs, Kafka correlation, Kubernetes status, redacted Hubble flows, and timestamps—not unsupported claims about production availability, throughput, or savings.

Explore the project: GitHub repository · Architecture · Adding an agent

entry.title: A Kubernetes Operator for Self-Hosted Cube Core
entry.summary: Deploy self-hosted Cube Core on Kubernetes, then query Kubernetes health and agent-execution telemetry: runs, skills, tools, handoffs, artifact references, validation, and model usage.
entry.content:
The Cube Core MicroK8s Operator encodes self-hosted Cube Core as a declarative Kubernetes API. A CubeCluster describes API replicas, refresh workers, Cube Store topology, model and Secret references, storage, and service exposure. The controller continuously turns that intent into standard Kubernetes resources and reports readiness back to the custom resource.

Despite its name, the operator is not tied to MicroK8s. It uses standard Kubernetes APIs on supported managed or self-hosted clusters; Proxmox and MicroK8s are optional infrastructure, not prerequisites. The current minimum Kubernetes version is 1.34. I use it in local cluster setups and on Kind.

Release scope: the public v0.1.0 alpha OLM catalog is installation-tested. The new agent-execution pipeline described below is prepared for the next source/release update; it is not in the published v0.1.0 image. The OperatorHub submission is under community review, not an available listing. The custom OLM catalog works independently of that review.

Why an operator instead of deployment YAML

A static manifest can start Cube, but it does not provide a durable ownership model. The operator validates referenced configuration, applies owner references, chooses single or clustered Cube Store resources, preserves allocated Service fields, removes resources made obsolete by topology changes, and calculates readiness from every expected component.

The platform.cube.dev/v1alpha1 API reconciles:

  • Cube API Deployment, Service, and PodDisruptionBudget;
  • a dedicated refresh-worker Deployment;
  • either one Cube Store Deployment or router/worker StatefulSets;
  • private services and a NetworkPolicy around Cube Store; and
  • a Ready condition with observed generation and internal endpoint.

The operator reads model ConfigMaps and configuration Secrets but does not create credentials. This keeps database passwords and JWT signing material out of custom-resource specs and Git history.

One API, two controller implementations

The default controller is written in Go with controller-runtime and Kubernetes Lease leader election. It is the recommended production path because multiple manager replicas can coordinate safely. A separately packaged Python/Kopf controller implements the same resource contract as a readable, Pythonic alternative for teams that prefer rapid Python iteration.

Exactly one implementation may run at a time. Both controllers own the same Deployments, Services, StatefulSets, and status fields; running both would create reconciliation races. Switching therefore means deleting one controller Deployment, waiting for termination, and only then applying the other.

The direct deployment guide covers Go/Kopf installation. Local image tags must be replaced with registry images outside Kind. The OLM route below uses the already-published Go image.

This dual implementation is useful beyond language preference: it documents which behavior belongs to the API contract and which belongs to a particular framework.

Install on Kubernetes

You need Kubernetes 1.34+, kubectl, classic OLM, a reachable PostgreSQL data source, and a default StorageClass or an existing suitable PVC. Your networking plugin must implement NetworkPolicy to enforce the Cube Store restrictions.

Install the public operator catalog

If classic OLM is absent, install Operator SDK and run operator-sdk olm install --version 0.46.0 --timeout 5m once. This uses classic OLM's CatalogSource and Subscription, not OLM v1. Do not run it alongside a direct Go or Kopf installation.

git clone https://github.com/sqe/cube-microk8s-operator.git
cd cube-microk8s-operator
kubectl apply -f config/olm/install.yaml
kubectl -n cube-system wait --for=create \
  csv/cube-microk8s-operator.v0.1.0 --timeout=5m
kubectl -n cube-system wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded \
  csv/cube-microk8s-operator.v0.1.0 --timeout=5m
kubectl -n cube-system rollout status deployment/cube-operator --timeout=2m

This installs the alpha Go controller cluster-wide in cube-system, not a Cube instance or a database. The manifest assumes the global catalog namespace is olm; adapt the CatalogSource namespace and Subscription's sourceNamespace if yours differs. Review its automatic InstallPlan approval policy before use; do not create a second OperatorGroup in an existing operator namespace. OperatorHub submission #9651 is a separate community review; OpenShift console listing is also separate.

Configure a model, credentials, and storage

This minimal model checks connectivity without depending on an application table. Replace it with semantic models for your own data afterward.

kubectl create namespace cube --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl -n cube apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: {name: cube-model}
data:
  Connectivity.yml: |
    cubes:
      - name: Connectivity
        sql: SELECT 1 AS id
        measures:
          - name: count
            type: count
        dimensions:
          - name: id
            sql: id
            type: number
            primary_key: true
YAML

# Bash: enter credentials interactively; never commit them.
read -rp 'PostgreSQL hostname: ' CUBE_DB_HOST
read -rp 'PostgreSQL database: ' CUBE_DB_NAME
read -rp 'PostgreSQL user: ' CUBE_DB_USER
read -rsp 'PostgreSQL password: ' CUBE_DB_PASS; echo
read -rsp 'Cube API signing secret: ' CUBE_API_SECRET; echo
kubectl -n cube create secret generic cube-configuration \
  --from-literal=CUBEJS_DB_TYPE=postgres \
  --from-literal=CUBEJS_DB_HOST="$CUBE_DB_HOST" \
  --from-literal=CUBEJS_DB_PORT=5432 \
  --from-literal=CUBEJS_DB_NAME="$CUBE_DB_NAME" \
  --from-literal=CUBEJS_DB_USER="$CUBE_DB_USER" \
  --from-literal=CUBEJS_DB_PASS="$CUBE_DB_PASS" \
  --from-literal=CUBEJS_API_SECRET="$CUBE_API_SECRET" \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
unset CUBE_DB_HOST CUBE_DB_NAME CUBE_DB_USER CUBE_DB_PASS CUBE_API_SECRET

kubectl -n cube apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: cube-remote}
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests: {storage: 10Gi}
---
apiVersion: platform.cube.dev/v1alpha1
kind: CubeCluster
metadata: {name: analytics}
spec:
  modelConfigMap: cube-model
  configurationSecret: cube-configuration
  api: {replicas: 2}
  refreshWorker: {replicas: 1}
  cubeStore:
    mode: single
    remoteStorage:
      type: persistentVolume
      persistentVolume: {existingClaim: cube-remote}
    scratch: {size: 2Gi}
  service: {type: ClusterIP}
YAML

Use an external secret manager and the database TLS settings appropriate for your provider in production. The operator does not provision PostgreSQL. The default Cube Store image is for amd64. On arm64, select the tested arm64 image before waiting for readiness:

kubectl -n cube patch cubecluster analytics --type=merge -p \
  '{"spec":{"cubeStore":{"image":"cubejs/cubestore:arm64v8@sha256:d9254a2166513e99f888da6f85362362357805116cd4d70f2b22e318e6ca5007"}}}'

Then, on either architecture:

kubectl -n cube wait --for=condition=Ready cubecluster/analytics --timeout=15m
kubectl -n cube get cubecluster analytics
kubectl -n cube port-forward --address 127.0.0.1 service/analytics-api 4000:4000
# In another terminal:
curl --fail --silent --show-error --max-time 10 http://127.0.0.1:4000/readyz

Health is unauthenticated. Metadata and queries require a short-lived Cube JWT, sent directly in Authorization without Bearer; see the REST examples. Public access needs your own TLS ingress and authorization policy. This compact single-store example is not an HA storage design.

Storage and query topology

Cube API translates dimensions and measures from the model ConfigMap into SQL for the configured data source. Cube Store serves caching and pre-aggregation; the refresh worker updates those structures independently from request-serving API replicas.

Single mode supports an ordinary existing PVC and is appropriate for compact installations. Clustered mode creates a router and multiple worker StatefulSets. Its remote directory must be genuinely shared and concurrently mountable, or it should use S3. Merely attaching the same ReadWriteOnce volume name to several nodes does not create a distributed filesystem.

apiVersion: platform.cube.dev/v1alpha1
kind: CubeCluster
metadata:
  name: analytics
  namespace: cube
spec:
  modelConfigMap: cube-model
  configurationSecret: cube-configuration
  api: {replicas: 2}
  refreshWorker: {replicas: 1}
  cubeStore:
    mode: clustered
    workers: 2
    remoteStorage:
      type: s3
      s3:
        bucket: company-cube-prod
        region: us-west-2
        secretRef: cubestore-s3

Default Cube/Cube Store images are digest-pinned. Workload identity is preferable for S3; a referenced Secret is available where static credentials are unavoidable. Containers drop Linux capabilities and disallow privilege escalation, while Cube Store accepts only the component traffic selected by NetworkPolicy.

A telemetry demo that tests more than installation

The Kind environment creates PostgreSQL, a read-only Node/Pod collector, Cube models, and Cube Core. The new update adds a separate authenticated ingestion service and the AgentExecutions model. The Go image runs the manager, collector, or ingestion as independent processes; event collection is not part of reconciliation.

# From the source checkout; requires Docker, Kind, kubectl, curl, jq and Python.
python -m pip install -r demo/requirements-mcp.txt
make kind-up       # Go controller
make kind-e2e
make kind-down

# The same demo through the Python implementation
make kind-up-kopf
make kind-e2e
make kind-down

The E2E checks exercise health, metadata, Kubernetes observations, and every execution-record kind through real Cube queries. A synthetic two-agent task has nine spans, two runs (one failed), one failed validation, 13,000 ms average run duration, 160 input tokens, 48 output tokens, and $0.0168 reported cost. These are test fixtures, not a claim that real agents performed those tasks. Checks cover bad credentials, invalid records, out-of-order delivery, duplicate retries, conflicting replays, and persistence after ingestion pod replacement. CI exercises Go and Kopf, including repeated setup, plus PostgreSQL integration tests and the Go race detector.

Kind detects amd64/arm64 and selects the matching Cube Store image. Access the demo at http://127.0.0.1:4000; ingestion is internal with temporary loopback forwarding during E2E. Production DNS, certificates, firewalls, backups, and ingress remain explicit environment responsibilities.

A real weather agent, not only a synthetic trace

I also ran the weather agent from my separate platform checkout through a standalone stdio MCP entrypoint. It uses the same Python WeatherHandler as the platform's Kafka weather service, but this demonstration invoked it on the host: it did not submit a Kafka task, run an LLM, or automatically instrument the entire deployed fleet. The agent fetched real data from Open-Meteo.

For the October 17, 2026 capture, Reykjavik's observation at 20:45 was:

{
  "location": "Reykjavik",
  "current": {
    "temperature_2m": 9.7,
    "relative_humidity_2m": 91,
    "wind_speed_10m": 45.0
  }
}

The units were °C, %, and km/h. These are captured values, not a current forecast or a performance benchmark. The completed trace mcp-bb768566719a424aba21b58af46a6c8b was ingested into PostgreSQL, then read back through Cube. Both returned the same BI metrics:

Agent Spans Runs Failed runs Average run ms Input/output tokens Reported USD
weather 3 1 0 2160.206 0 / 0 0

The three successful records describe the run, the MCP tool call, and the JSON result artifact reference. No model ran, so tokens and cost are zero—not estimated or fabricated. A new invocation gets its own trace ID and real timestamps.

The operator repository's MCP execution client can invoke a trusted stdio MCP server, save its actual response and completed spans, submit them to ingestion, and verify the returned Cube graph. An --execute-only mode explicitly skips ingestion and reports cubeVerified: false; the full capture above reported cubeVerified: true. The private agent implementation is not copied into the public operator repo. See the reproduction guide for environment setup, token handling, and commands.

What is stored in SQL, and what is semantic?

The execution records are physically persisted in public.agent_executions: identities, parent links, timestamps, outcomes, duration, usage, and typed detail fields in JSONB. The weather response itself is a local .result.json artifact; SQL stores its URI and media type, not normalized temperature or humidity observations. A file: URI is local to that host, not an uploaded report or a portable download link.

Cube's AgentExecutions.yml defines the semantic measures and dimensions. When a client requests runs or latency, Cube generates SQL over the stored events. It does not create a materialized SQL table for every measure. The verified /cubejs-api/v1/sql response reported external: false and preAggregations: []: this demo queried PostgreSQL without a pre-aggregation. Deploying Cube Store does not, by itself, prove caching or rollup acceleration.

For an authorized database audit, this query reproduces the captured run count and average latency:

SELECT agent_name,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'run') AS runs,
       avg(duration_ms) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'run') AS average_run_ms
FROM public.agent_executions
WHERE trace_id = 'mcp-bb768566719a424aba21b58af46a6c8b'
GROUP BY agent_name;

It returned weather, 1, and 2160.206. The corresponding Cube REST query lets BI applications use the shared semantic definitions instead of reimplementing that SQL in every consumer:

{
  "query": {
    "dimensions": ["AgentExecutions.agent"],
    "measures": ["AgentExecutions.runs", "AgentExecutions.averageRunDurationMs"],
    "filters": [{
      "member": "AgentExecutions.traceId", "operator": "equals",
      "values": ["mcp-bb768566719a424aba21b58af46a6c8b"]
    }]
  }
}

Post this to /cubejs-api/v1/load with a short-lived Cube JWT in Authorization. For daily execution BI, group by agent and day using AgentExecutions.endedAt, then compare run counts, failures, latency, and reported model usage. For audit drill-down, query event/parent IDs, tool names, and artifact URIs. Do not sum overlapping span durations as total run latency. The query guide includes the full aggregate query, raw-record SQL, and inspection of Cube's generated SQL. Retention applies, so replace the captured trace ID with a fresh one when reproducing the example.

This is BI about agent execution, not yet weather-domain BI. Analyzing temperature trends would require a separate observation table and Cube model. Nor does this configure a dashboard product or expose Cube's SQL wire protocol. The shared-token demo is not tenant isolation: server-side access policies are still required before external or multi-tenant use.

Public CI exercises the MCP → ingestion → PostgreSQL → Cube path for both controllers with a clearly labelled deterministic fixture. It does not depend on my private checkout or the availability of a live weather API. The live weather run and matching SQL/Cube results were verified separately.

Concrete artifacts: infrastructure versus agent output

For CubeCluster/analytics in single-store mode, the operator creates analytics-api (Deployment, Service, and PDB), analytics-refresh-worker (Deployment), analytics-cubestore (Deployment and Service), and a Cube Store NetworkPolicy. Clustered mode substitutes router/worker StatefulSets and Services. These are inspectable Kubernetes objects with owner references:

kubectl -n cube get deployments,statefulsets,services,pdb,networkpolicy
kubectl -n cube get cubecluster analytics -o yaml

The optional telemetry service creates the agent_executions PostgreSQL table; the demo provides AgentExecutions.yml in the model ConfigMap. Cube generates source SQL when clients query the model. The operator itself neither authors application SQL nor creates reports, screenshots, or code patches.

Agents create those output artifacts. The telemetry service records their references and context. A completed artifact record could look like this (illustrative IDs/timestamps, not a real published report):

{
  "eventId": "task-123-artifact",
  "traceId": "task-123",
  "runId": "task-123-analytics",
  "parentId": "task-123-analytics",
  "tenantId": "local",
  "cluster": "kind-cube-demo",
  "namespace": "cube-demo",
  "agent": "analytics-worker",
  "kind": "artifact",
  "name": "usage-report",
  "status": "succeeded",
  "artifactUri": "urn:example:task-123:usage-report",
  "artifactType": "application/json",
  "startedAt": "2026-10-17T10:00:00Z",
  "endedAt": "2026-10-17T10:00:01Z"
}

This may reference an agent-produced report, SQL file, test result, code patch, or screenshot stored elsewhere. Ingestion neither fetches nor stores the file; never send private content, credentials, or signed download URLs as metadata.

What we capture for a complete agent task

Agents instrument their runtime and submit terminal records to POST /v1/executions, authenticated with a separate ingestion token. Each record has an event ID, trace/run/parent links, agent, timestamps, and an outcome.

Record Captured evidence
Run Agent identity, task name, success/failure/cancellation, latency.
Skill Skill name/version and its parent run.
Tool Tool identity, outcome, duration, parent skill or run.
Handoff Target agent; a delegated run links to the handoff.
Artifact URI and media type, not the artifact contents.
Validation Check name and passed/failed/skipped outcome.
Model call Provider/model, input/output tokens, reported USD cost.

For example: an analytics worker runs operating-cube-core, calls a Cube query tool, records a report URI, and hands review to a second agent. The reviewer records its own run, model call, and validation result. All share a trace ID, with parent IDs showing how work was nested or delegated. This answers “which agents ran, what skills/tools did they use, what did they produce, and how did verification turn out?” without collecting private reasoning.

Usage belongs only to model-call records, preventing double-counted run totals. Immutable IDs make identical delivery retries safe and reject changed replays. Retention defaults to seven days. Costs are producer-reported, not calculated billing. A Cube query can compare outcomes and usage by agent:

{
  "query": {
    "measures": ["AgentExecutions.runs", "AgentExecutions.failedRuns", "AgentExecutions.inputTokens", "AgentExecutions.outputTokens", "AgentExecutions.costUsd"],
    "dimensions": ["AgentExecutions.agent"],
    "limit": 100
  }
}

The synthetic E2E task's expected usage rows are:

[
  {"agent": "analytics-worker", "runs": 1, "failedRuns": 0, "inputTokens": 137, "outputTokens": 41, "costUsd": 0.0123},
  {"agent": "reviewer", "runs": 1, "failedRuns": 1, "inputTokens": 23, "outputTokens": 7, "costUsd": 0.0045}
]

These are readable projections of expected semantic results; Cube's actual responses use qualified member names such as AgentExecutions.runs and commonly encode numeric values as strings. Filter by trace ID to inspect one task, or by kind = skill and group by name/version to compare skill outcomes.

Inspect /cubejs-api/v1/meta before querying. The execution contract has submission examples and the complete field contract. This is not automatic agent discovery, a live workflow engine, or chain-of-thought collection; it requires no Kafka or Temporal. The local shared-token endpoint is not a multi-tenant security boundary: external use requires trusted identity, server-side tenant enforcement, TLS, network restrictions, and rate limits.

Agents consume governed analytics, not database credentials

A local read-only agent skill uses a short-lived Cube JWT supplied by a trusted caller and calls the Cube Core REST contract. It first inspects /cubejs-api/v1/meta, then submits bounded semantic queries to /cubejs-api/v1/load. This lets an agent use named measures and dimensions without receiving PostgreSQL credentials or permission to execute arbitrary SQL through the skill. Authentication, allowed models, and tenant filters still require explicit server-side policy; the operator does not configure OIDC or guarantee tenant isolation by itself.

Cube's hosted Chat API and official Cloud skills are a separate product boundary. This project documents them as optional Cube Cloud integrations; it does not claim those hosted features are part of open-source Cube Core.

Operational and licensing boundaries

Before production use, test CRD upgrades, restore procedures, controller failover, Cube Store recovery, database limits, and model changes under the target workload. “Production-oriented” means these controls are represented; it does not replace environment-specific qualification. The next catalog is for fresh installations, not an advertised automatic upgrade from v0.1.0.

This is an independent community project, not an official Cube product or a claim of Cube endorsement. It deploys upstream Cube and Cube Store images; credit belongs to the Cube authors and contributors. Original operator code is Apache-2.0. Cube Client is MIT licensed; Cube Backend is Apache-2.0 licensed. Upstream licenses/notices remain separate and must be preserved when redistributing those components.

Explore the project: GitHub repository · Architecture · Execution telemetry · Agent boundary

entry.title: Model Fleet: Declarative GPU Inference, Training, and Agent Operations
entry.summary: A deep technical look at a Kubernetes operator that converts model intent into standard inference, training, networking, scaling, dataset, GPU-placement, observability, and agent-control resources.
entry.content:
The Model Fleet Operator provides one declarative API for containerized inference, training, immutable datasets, and managed agents. The central principle is deliberately conservative: custom resources express intent, while the resulting workloads remain ordinary Kubernetes Deployments, Services, Jobs, KEDA scalers, and Cilium routes.

Four APIs divide ownership cleanly

InferenceService describes a model-serving container, resource requests, accelerator fit, scaling policy, Service, and optional Gateway API route. TrainingRun creates one immutable Job attempt with datasets, storage, deadlines, retries, parallelism, suspension, and cancellation. Dataset registers immutable version metadata, named splits, an access allowlist, and an optional read-only PVC. AgentRegistration links a versioned Agent Card to its runtime and operational state.

This avoids model-specific shell scripts while preserving Kubernetes debugging:

kubectl apply -f examples/inference-vllm.yaml
kubectl get isvc,deploy,service,scaledobject,httproute -n models

kubectl apply -f examples/training-pytorch.yaml
kubectl get trun,job -n models

The controller never downloads model data into its own pod and never reads a Hugging Face token. An init container can prefetch into a shared volume using a Secret reference; the inference container sees only the resulting model files. Training outputs and checkpoints belong in durable object storage, not the Job's ephemeral filesystem.

GPU fit is a scheduling input, not a performance promise

Requesting one GPU says nothing about whether a model fits. Model Fleet accepts module-level budgets split into sharded and replicated memory. Sharded weights are divided across the requested GPU count; runtime libraries and other replicated allocations are added per device, then a safety margin is applied:

required per GPU = ceil((Σ sharded / GPU count + Σ replicated) × (1 + margin))

For 90 GiB of sharded allocations, 4 GiB replicated per device, two GPUs, and a 10% margin, each GPU needs ceil((90 / 2 + 4) × 1.10) = 54 GiB. The operator maps that requirement to a portable GPU-memory capacity label and can also add required affinity for specific NVIDIA products.

This is admission and placement guidance—not dynamic VRAM bin packing and not a throughput guarantee. Kubernetes still allocates whole GPU devices. Drivers, device plugins, MIG configuration, and node labels remain infrastructure responsibilities, owned by cloud images or the NVIDIA GPU Operator.

Pod scaling and node capacity are different control loops

KEDA decides how many model pods are needed. A cloud or bare-metal capacity provider decides whether nodes exist to run pending pods. Keeping those loops separate makes the workload API portable:

  • EKS can use Karpenter NodePools;
  • GKE can use managed node-pool autoscaling; and
  • bare metal uses existing NVIDIA nodes or an external machine provider.

True scale-to-zero requires a signal that exists while the model pod is absent, such as Kafka lag, gateway backlog, SQS, or Pub/Sub. A Prometheus metric emitted only by the sleeping model cannot wake itself. This detail is why the operator passes through external KEDA triggers rather than inventing a misleading “automatic” scaler.

Cilium networking and secure workload boundaries

An InferenceService creates an HTTPRoute; the platform administrator owns the shared Cilium Gateway, listener policy, certificates, and public DNS. This keeps model authors from silently creating load balancers. Dedicated service accounts and Secret references keep provider, registry, and repository credentials outside the operator and custom-resource status.

The same chart runs on Kind, MicroK8s, EKS, and GKE when Cilium owns Gateway API. Kind intentionally uses an echo workload because Docker nodes do not expose a GPU by default; it verifies controller reconciliation and L7 routing without pretending to benchmark inference.

git clone https://github.com/sqe/model-fleet-operator.git
cd model-fleet-operator
make kind-up
kubectl --context kind-model-fleet apply -f examples/inference-kind.yaml
curl -H 'Host: model.localhost' http://127.0.0.1:8080/
make kind-down

The agent and operations control plane

The optional registry persists Agent Cards as AgentRegistration resources. The supervisor resolves an exact skill or asks an allowlisted LLM gateway to choose among registered skills, then publishes JSON-RPC through Kafka. Workers publish a correlated result before committing the task. A built-in operations agent can inspect fleet state and request explicit inference or training actions using the same contract.

Slack uses Socket Mode, so the bot needs no public callback ingress. Read-only inventory is the safe default. Mutating operations require user/channel allowlists, and quota requests are disabled until a reviewed provider policy is attached. Sensitive commands require explicit confirmation rather than treating natural language as authorization.

Operational visibility combines Prometheus, Grafana, Hubble, DCGM GPU metrics, OpenCost, cloud billing exports, and MLflow. Billing and OpenCost can overlap, so the reporting path presents them separately instead of adding them into a misleading total. Grafana snapshots can stream to Slack without writing PNGs to the bot filesystem.

Concrete Qwen patterns

The examples include a quantized Qwen 27B inference/gateway profile and a Qwen3-VL image LoRA training shape. Quantization reduces weight memory but does not make KV cache, activations, runtime allocations, context length, or training memory disappear. A 24 GiB target is a testable fit hypothesis; production capacity must be measured on the exact GPU, driver, serving build, sequence length, and concurrency. The operator captures those requirements without hard-coding one model family.

The result is a control plane with clear boundaries: model authors declare workloads and immutable inputs, Kubernetes reconciles pods and Jobs, KEDA owns replica demand, infrastructure owns nodes, Cilium owns ingress, and observability systems provide evidence. Each component can be replaced without rewriting the custom-resource contract.
